bib.title: Intrinsic Dimensionality Explains the Effectiveness of Language Model Fine-Tuning
bib.venue: ACL-IJCNLP 2021 (Proceedings of the 59th Annual Meeting of the ACL, pages 7319-7328)

question: Why can pretrained language models with hundreds of millions of parameters be fine-tuned with plain gradient descent on only hundreds or thousands of labeled examples?
hypothesis: Pre-training implicitly lowers the intrinsic dimension (minimal description length) of the average NLP task, and lower intrinsic dimension means better generalization.
contributions: Common NLP tasks within pre-trained representations have an intrinsic dimension several orders of magnitude less than the full parameterization.
Interpret intrinsic dimension as the fine-tuning task's minimal description length within the pre-trained model; pre-training implicitly optimizes it over the average of NLP tasks.
Measure intrinsic dimension of many pre-trained models; larger models tend to have smaller intrinsic dimension.
Compression-based generalization bounds applied to the intrinsic-dimension framework give bounds independent of pre-trained parameter count.

method.summary: Fine-tunes a pretrained model only inside a d-dimensional random subspace (theta = theta0 + P(theta_d), Fastfood projection, optionally with per-layer scaling, SAID) and finds the smallest d reaching 90% of full fine-tuning accuracy (d90). Applied to BERT/RoBERTa on MRPC and QQP, to a RoBERTa-Base re-pretrained from scratch (checkpoints every 10k updates, six tasks), and to 18 public models on MRPC.

training.objective: fine-tuning (task loss) in subspace theta = theta0 + theta_d M, M = HG Pi HB (Fastfood); SAID: theta_i = theta0_i + lambda_i P(theta_{d-m})_i with m layer scales learned jointly; classification head also optimised inside the d parameters
training.lr: small search across four learning rates per training run (values not given)

other.theta_d_init: zero vector, so start equals the pre-trained model
other.sec4_sweep: 100 subspace trainings per dataset and model, d from 10 to 10000 on a log scale
other.sec5_1_d90_search: binary search over d per checkpoint, min 100, max 4 million; reuse best learning rates from Sec 4 for d < 10000, fixed learning rate otherwise
other.d90_definition: smallest d reaching 0.9 x full fine-tuning metric (e.g. 85% -> 76.5%)
other.full_solution: fine-tune the checkpoint in the standard way
other.sec5_2: same binary search on MRPC with extra small learning-rate searches per model
other.optimizer_note: 'standard SGD' mentioned in Sec 3; optimizer not otherwise named

inference.samples: single run per (d, model, dataset); no seeds or repeats stated

limits: d90 is an upper bound from random Fastfood projections; the authors say the true intrinsic dimension is likely much lower.
The generalization bound applies only to models trained in the intrinsic subspace; the authors say it is not shown that standard SGD optimises in this space.
Fixed-method size sweep (same pre-training, varying size) was infeasible; the size trend mixes pre-training methods.
Only sentence-classification tasks; no generation tasks, no models above T5-3B.
Optimizer, batch size, steps, learning-rate values, seeds and variance are not reported; no code link.
Per-dataset parameter-count trends are said to be in the Appendix, which in this PDF contains only the proof.
Fig 2 is missing d90 points for checkpoints where full fine-tuning stayed at majority-class accuracy or SAID was unstable.
Correlations between d90 and generalization are shown in plots only, with no statistics.
